props.title: Lilies of the Field
props.initialSlug: One man, a mountain of faith.

sections.content: Lilies of the Field marks a groundbreaking moment in cinema history, featuring Sidney Poitier's Oscar-winning performance as Homer Smith - the first Black actor to win Best Actor. The film's deceptively simple story of a traveling handyman helping German nuns build a chapel in the Arizona desert becomes a masterclass in subtle social commentary and cross-cultural understanding. Director Ralph Nelson crafts a narrative that echoes similar faith-based wanderer tales like The Fugitive (1947) but revolutionizes the genre by centering a Black protagonist in a role of agency and dignity during the Civil Rights era.

sections.content: The film's influence ripples through later religious-themed character studies like Tender Mercies (1983) and Dead Man Walking (1995), where faith intersects with personal redemption. Poitier's naturalistic performance style, blending humor with quiet dignity, set new standards for character-driven drama. The film's approach to depicting religious faith - respectful but never preachy - created a template for how to handle spiritual themes in mainstream cinema.

The technical achievements of Lilies of the Field are often overlooked. Ernest Haller's black-and-white cinematography transforms the Arizona desert into a character itself, while the minimal score by Jerry Goldsmith emphasizes the spiritual nature of the story without overwhelming it. The film's economical 95-minute runtime and focused narrative influenced later independent filmmakers like John Sayles in works like Brother from Another Planet (1984). sections.content: The film's handling of racial issues through subtext rather than direct confrontation created a new paradigm for social issue films. While contemporaneous films like The Defiant Ones (1958) dealt with race head-on, Lilies of the Field demonstrated how integration could be portrayed as natural and unremarkable. This approach influenced later films like Glory (1989) and Driving Miss Daisy (1989), which similarly explored racial themes through character-driven narratives.
